problem: LLM-based navigation agents transcribe spoken instructions to text and assume the human command is reliable, discarding vocal cues (pitch, loudness, speech rate) that signal uncertainty. They therefore follow hesitant or wrong guidance and fail to reach the target.
motivation: Humans judge the credibility of spoken directions from tone and hesitation as well as words, and in unfamiliar spaces their guidance is often vague. A robot that ignores this will follow doubtful guidance blindly, so it needs to model semantic and vocal uncertainty, then fall back on its own perception or ask for help.
key_idea: Feed Whisper transcripts plus extracted vocal cues (pitch, loudness, speech rate) into an LLM that does chain-of-thought multiple-choice planning, and when the command is judged uncertain, override it with the robot's own visual scene-direction conjecture or ask a human.
insight: Vocal cues add information that text lacks: the text-only LLM reaches 22.16% PSSR, CoT alone 49.30%, and adding all three vocal cues 70.46%, with the largest gain on vocal-uncertainty clips (VU). In RoboTHOR, removing the vocal module drops SR to 25% (LU) and 50% (VU) versus 80% for the full model. Removing vision raises SPL, because perception-driven exploration lengthens paths, but it lowers success. Uncertainty from vocal cues also makes the agent robust to a paraphrase attack that swaps uncertain words for confident ones.
method: Audio uncertainty modeling: Whisper transcribes the audio; the LLM detects semantic disfluencies (ambiguous word choice, speech repair, hesitation). Vocal features (maximum loudness change, pitch shift, per-segment speech rate) are extracted and aligned to the text by forced alignment.

MCQA task planning: The prompt combines text and cues, with CoT and 3 in-context examples (text-uncertain, vocal-uncertain, both). The LLM proposes 5 options: A is the literal paraphrase, B-D acknowledge uncertainty, E is 'ask another person'. The option with the highest next-token log-probability is selected.

Visual scene direction conjecture: When the chosen step is ambiguous, the robot looks left, front and right, categorizes the detected objects, and infers which direction likely contains the target (e.g. TV implies the remote control is near). It follows this inference instead of the human direction, or asks a human if few objects are visible.
Tool library: Voyager-style function calls (move_forward_to_target, turn_left, etc.) convert LLM plans to robot actions, using off-the-shelf object detection and depth estimation.
Confidence score: C(rho)=1/KL(rho, rho*), where rho* is a delta on the annotated optimal option, used together with PSSR to measure uncertainty calibration.
Real-world stack: YOLOv8 for objects, Tesseract for text/signs, MiDaS for depth.

results: On DNIA, PSSR is 70.46% versus 22.16% for a text-only LLM and 49.30% for CoT. In RoboTHOR, SR is 80% on both LU and VU versus 25% for LM-Nav and random search. After a token attack, PSSR falls by 33.43% relative for TrustNavGPT versus 55.87% for LM-Nav + few-shot.
limitations: Vocal and semantic analysis adds computational overhead, which limits real-time or low-resource deployment
Depends on clean audio quality; recordings were made in quiet environments
